name: Understanding loop performance
description: Why does a loop take the time it takes? Latency and throughput bounds, simulation and timeline, with optional in-depth cards.

steps.title: Welcome to RVCAT
steps.description:
RVCAT explains why a loop takes the time it takes.
It simulates a loop running on a configurable out-of-order processor
and answers one question: how many cycles does each iteration need?

At each topic you can continue, or open an In depth card first.

steps.title: The loop program
steps.description:
One iteration of the loop, written as simple machine instructions.
The loop runs N times (N is set next to the program name).
For performance, what matters is the instruction types
and the data dependences between instructions.

steps.title: In depth: the program
steps.description:
• The type button cycles the columns: operand sizes, latency and
   ports, inputs/outputs, memory addresses, strides and vector lanes.
• Pick another program in the list, or edit it with ✎ (or Edit Program).
• Not modeled: registers, branch outcomes and memory ordering.
• After a simulation, the first column shows how much each
   instruction contributes to the critical path.

steps.title: The processor
steps.description:
A pipeline described by a few numbers.
• Dispatch / Retire: instructions per cycle that enter / leave.
• Ports P0…Pn: each executes 1 instruction per cycle, of the types listed.
• ROB: how many instructions can be in flight at the same time.
• Cache (optional): adds the delays of memory accesses.

steps.title: In depth: the processor
steps.description:
• Click 🔄 in the diagram to change dispatch, retire, ROB or cache.
• Scheduler: greedy issues the oldest ready instructions;
   optimal chooses the best combination of ports.
• Cache: blocks × block size, miss penalty, issue time, fill and
   write buffers, and return throughput.
• Edit Processor (top bar) changes latencies and ports.

steps.title: Two bounds on performance
steps.description:
Minimum time = max( latency bound , throughput bound ).
• Latency bound: a chain of dependent instructions that repeats
   every iteration cannot run faster than the sum of its latencies.
• Throughput bound: the busiest resource (dispatch, retire or a set
   of ports) cannot do more work per cycle.
The larger bound tells you what limits the loop.

steps.title: Latency bounds
steps.description:
Each row is a cyclic chain of dependences.
Cycles/iter = sum of latencies ÷ loop iterations spanned by the chain.
The row tagged max gives the latency bound.
Tip: click a row to see that chain in the dependence graph.

steps.title: In depth: the dependence graph
steps.description:
• 📈 Dependence graph opens a movable, resizable window.
• One box per loop iteration; cyclic dependences are drawn in red.
• Clicking a row of Latency bounds highlights its chain.
• Hovering an instruction number highlights it in the graph and program.
• Mouse wheel: zoom · drag: move · Fit: whole graph.

steps.title: Throughput bounds
steps.description:
Each row is a resource and the work it must do.
Cycles/iter = instructions that can only use it ÷ its throughput.
The row tagged max gives the throughput bound.
Hover (or click) a value to see how it is computed.

steps.title: In depth: sets of ports
steps.description:
• An instruction that can run on P0 or P2 does not load P0 alone:
   it only counts for sets that contain both ports.
• Numbers in grey are instructions that can escape to
   another port (hover to see which ones).
• Sets of ports are listed when they share instructions:
   P0+P2 and P2+P3 give P0+P2+P3.

steps.title: Check: which bound?
steps.questionText: A loop has a latency bound of 5.00 and a throughput bound of 2.33 cycles/iter. What is its minimum time per iteration?

answers.explanation: Right: the slowest constraint wins, max(5.00, 2.33) = 5.00.

answers.text: 2.33 cycles/iter: out-of-order execution hides the latency
answers.explanation: Out-of-order execution overlaps iterations, but a cyclic chain still needs 5 cycles per iteration.
The bounds do not add: they are two independent lower limits, and the larger one applies.

answers.text: 3.67 cycles/iter: the average of both bounds
answers.explanation: There is no averaging: the minimum time is the maximum of the bounds.

steps.title: Run the simulation
steps.description:
Now measure it: click Run Simulation.
Compare Cycles/iter with the minimum time of the static analysis:
• close to it: the bounds explain the performance;
• much higher: something else slows the loop (memory, scheduling, ROB).

steps.title: In depth: simulation results
steps.description:
• IPC: instructions per cycle (its colour shows dispatch usage).
• Primary misses start a block fill; secondary ones join a fill in progress.
• MM transfers: main-memory reads + writes, and % of cycles busy.
• The diagram shows how busy dispatch, each port, the cache and retire are.
• Store Results keeps a run; click its name to see program, N and processor.

steps.title: The timeline
steps.description:
Cycle by cycle: what each instruction is doing.
Rows are instructions (one colour per iteration), columns are cycles:
D dispatch · E execute · W write result · R retire.
The symbols in between show why an instruction waits.
Critical marks the chain that determines the execution time.

steps.title: In depth: waiting symbols
steps.description:
• . waits for a source operand (data dependence)
• * waits for a free port (port conflict)
• - already executed, waits for older instructions to retire
• With a cache: ! cache/MM slot · : block fill · 2 fill in progress
   · @ cache return queue
• Ports and Cache add rows with resource usage; Fit fills the width.

steps.title: Check: reading the timeline
steps.questionText: An instruction shows D . . . E W R in the timeline. Why does it wait after being dispatched?

answers.text: It waits for a source operand produced by an older instruction
answers.explanation: Yes: "." means a data dependence; it executes (E) when the operand is ready.

answers.text: It waits for a free execution port
answers.explanation: A port conflict is shown with "*".

answers.text: It waits for older instructions to retire
answers.explanation: That is "-", and it appears after the result is written (W).

answers.text: It waits for a cache miss
answers.explanation: Cache waits are shown with "!", ":", "2" or "@".

steps.title: Experiment!
steps.description:
Change one thing, predict the effect, then simulate.
• Edit the program or the processor (top bar), or change N.
• Add a port, change a latency or the ROB size.
• Store Results to compare runs side by side.
Tip: click any value with an explanation to pin it.
The ? button (bottom right) reopens the tutorials.
